newsitem.title: USA: Dunavant sees world cotton crop at 87.2 mln bales.
newsitem.headline: Dunavant sees world cotton crop at 87.2 mln bales.

text.p: Cotton merchant William B. Dunavant Jr. forecast U.S. 1997/98 cotton production at 18.2 million bales and world production at 87.2 million bales.
Speaking at a World Cotton Conference organized by Rabobank International, Dunavant said he saw U.S. 1997/98 planted cotton acreage at 14 million acres against 14,665,000 acres last season.
Using average yields and five percent abandonment, "...then we are on target for 18.2 million bales of production," he said.

Dunavant predicted U.S. consumption was on target for 11.2 million bales in 1997/98 against 11 million this season and projected exports of 7 million bales for total offtake of 18.2 million bales, the same as his projected production.

He projected U.S. carryover for the 1997/98 to be in a range of 3.8 to 4.1 million bales, the same as he projected for this marketing year. The U.S. carryover this season would vary with the price level over the next four months, he said. If the U.S. price stayed high over the next four months he believed the U.S. carryover would be closer to the 4.1 million bale level than 3.8 million.
Dunavant projected world cotton acreage to be about 83.7 million acres in 1997/98 against 84.1 million last season and said this should produce 87.2 million bales.
With current price levels, he projected that world cotton consumption in 1997/98 would escalate to 87.3 million bales from this year's level of about 85.5 million bales.
He projected that world carryover would basically remain unchanged for 1997/98 compared to this season but said weather conditions over the next eight months could change that.

In the prepared text of his speech, Dunavant said he believed December cotton was fairly priced between 77 and 78 cents based on normal yields around the world and the current price of manmade fibers.

He said his company was focusing on three factors to give it a price signal in the short term -- demand, which he said was currently satisfactory for U.S. cotton; the harvest of the southern hemisphere crops, particularly Australia; and the planting in April and May of the northern hemisphere crops.
"Any major problem in any of these areas will drive prices higher," he said.
